title: Database Migrations and Seeding
learning_outcomes: Explain how database migrations and seeding affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from version-controlled schema changes to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on database migrations and seeding in databases and persistence. You will connect version-controlled schema changes to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Database Migrations and Seeding matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying version-controlled schema changes deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Database constraints and transaction boundaries protect data integrity when requests fail or race with one another. In this lesson, treat “Database Migrations and Seeding” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

  id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  owner_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  title TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(title) BETWEEN 1 AND 200),

content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating database migrations and seeding as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
